Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries

Craft the prompt, reuse the template, manage the library. Build a shared collection of prompts that teams can find, test, version, and improve.

Explore the slides

From a single instruction to a shared library

Prompt engineering focuses on clear, effective instructions. Templates preserve that structure while allowing inputs to change. Libraries add the management practices needed to reuse those templates across applications and teams.

Three levels of prompt maturity
LevelPurposeKey question
PromptGuide a model on a specific taskIs the instruction clear and complete?
TemplateReuse structure with variable inputsDoes it work across different inputs?
LibraryManage shared prompts and templatesCan teams find, trust, and improve it?

What belongs in a prompt library entry?

Give every entry a domain/task identifier, an accountable owner, a description, and consistent tags. Store the template and its declared variables alongside model settings, evaluation evidence, and a changelog. Keep shared tone guides and output rules in reusable blocks.

A lifecycle with evidence at each step

  1. Draft: write the prompt and representative test cases.
  2. Evaluate: compare quality, safety, cost, and latency with a baseline.
  3. Review: check the change with domain and safety reviewers.
  4. Publish: point the production label at the approved version.
  5. Monitor: record usage, feedback, and operational results.
  6. Improve or retire: create a new version or remove unused entries from active use.

Versioning and governance

Preserve immutable versions and use environment labels to select approved versions. Pin exact versions when reproducibility matters. Separate editing from publishing, keep secrets out of templates, limit tool permissions, validate outputs, and record which prompt version produced each result.

Begin with a handful of frequently used prompts: inventory them, assign owners, add test sets, centralize the entries, and establish review practices before growing the collection.

Slide 4: Prompt Engineering in Brief

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Prompt Engineering in Brief Designing inputs that reliably produce the outputs you need Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 4 Prompt engineering is designing effective inputs (prompts) that guide large language models to the desired output. It is a fundamental skill for using LLMs across diverse applications. Clarity State the task or query clearly. Context Give enough background for an accurate response. Structure Use formatting and delimiters to aid interpretation. Specificity Specify the expected output format and details. Iteration Refine continuously based on results and feedback. Each dimension is covered in depth in the Dimensions of Prompt Engineering module.

Slide 5: Prompt Templates in Brief

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Prompt Templates in Brief Reusable patterns with placeholders for dynamic variables Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 5 Prompt templates are reusable patterns that standardize prompt design for specific tasks. Placeholders for dynamic variables make them flexible and scalable across scenarios. Summarize {document} for {audience} in {n} bullet points. Tone: {tone}. Modularity Adapts to different tasks with minimal changes. Flexibility Handles varied inputs and dynamic variables. Reusability Standardizes prompts, reducing repeated effort. Scalability Extends to complex workflows and many scenarios. Optimization Improves over time through testing and tuning.

Slide 6: What Is a Prompt Library?

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
What Is a Prompt Library? A shared, governed home for prompts and templates Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 6 A prompt library is a collection of pre-designed prompts and templates, organized by task or domain. It is the repository for efficient reuse and for experimenting with prompt designs. Authors Prompt engineers and domain experts write, test and submit prompts Prompt library support/ triage · reply-draft marketing/ blog-outline · social-post analytics/ kpi-summary · sql-explain shared/ tone-guide · json-rules Consumers Applications, agents and people fetch the approved version by name

Slide 7: Benefits of a Prompt Library

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Benefits of a Prompt Library What changes when prompts become shared assets Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 7 Efficiency Saves time by reusing proven prompts. WITHOUT A LIBRARY Every team rewrites the same prompt from scratch. Consistency Uniform behaviour and tone across applications. WITHOUT A LIBRARY Five chatbots, five tones, five policies. Experimentation Makes A/B testing of prompt versions routine. WITHOUT A LIBRARY No baseline to compare a change against. Knowledge sharing Centralizes expertise so the whole team can use it. WITHOUT A LIBRARY The best prompts live in one person's notes. Scalability Supports rapid expansion of LLM applications. WITHOUT A LIBRARY Copies drift apart; nobody knows which is live.

Slide 8: Anatomy of a Library Entry

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Anatomy of a Library Entry Everything needed to find, trust and reuse a prompt Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 8 id: support/triage owner: support-ai-team description: Classify tickets by category and priority tags: [support, classification, json] labels: {production: "1.2.0", staging: "1.3.0"} versions: "1.2.0": model: {provider: default, temperature: 0} variables: [company, categories, ticket_text] template: | You are a support triage assistant for {company}. Classify the ticket into one of: {categories}. Ticket: """{ticket_text}""" Return JSON with category and priority. eval: {dataset: triage-golden-v3, accuracy: 0.94} changelog: Added priority; stricter JSON rule 1 Identity and ownership id, owner, description and tags make it findable and accountable. 2 Labels Movable pointers decide which version each environment uses. 3 Model settings The model and parameters the prompt was tested with. 4 Template and variables The reusable text plus its declared inputs. 5 Evidence and history Eval results and a changelog for every version.

Organizing the Library Make the right prompt easy to find and safe to reuse Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 9 prompts/ support/ └ triage └ reply-draft marketing/ └ blog-outline analytics/ └ kpi-summary shared/ └ tone-guide (reusable block) └ json-rules (reusable block) Name by domain and task A predictable pattern such as domain/task, used everywhere. Tag consistently Task type, model, language and risk level, from a short controlled list. Share common blocks Tone guides, safety rules and output formats written once and referenced. Make it searchable Description, owner and example inputs on every entry.

Slide 11: Versioning and Labels

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Versioning and Labels Deploy by moving a label; roll back by moving it back Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 11 v1 v2 v3 v4 v5 v6 v7 production staging Versions are immutable snapshots. Labels (also called aliases or tags) are movable pointers. 1 Immutable versions Every change creates a new version you can diff and reproduce. 2 Labels for environments production, staging and dev point at specific versions. 3 Deploy without redeploying Apps fetch by label, so promotion needs no code release. 4 Instant rollback Point production back at the previous version. 5 Pin when it matters Regulated or high-risk flows reference an exact version. Same idea, different names Langfuse calls them labels, MLflow Prompt Registry calls them aliases, and LangSmith uses commit tags. In Git, a release tag or branch plays the same role.

Slide 12: Evaluating Library Prompts

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Evaluating Library Prompts Every version earns its place with evidence Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 12 Quality • Accuracy on a golden test set • Format and schema adherence • Human or LLM-judge ratings Safety • Resistance to prompt injection • No leakage of sensitive data • Correct refusals Cost and latency • Tokens per call • Response time under load • Cost per successful task Usage and feedback • Calls per prompt version • User ratings and escalations • Unused entries to retire Promotion rule: run the eval set on every new version and every model upgrade; promote only if it beats the current production version.

Slide 13: In Code: Using a Prompt Registry

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
In Code: Using a Prompt Registry Fetch by label, fill variables, promote safely (Langfuse example) Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 13 from langfuse import get_client langfuse = get_client() # 1. Fetch the version labelled "production" (cached client-side) prompt = langfuse.get_prompt("support/triage", label="production") # 2. Fill the template's variables text = prompt.compile(company="Acme Cloud", categories="billing, bug, how-to, account", ticket_text=ticket) # 3. Use the model settings stored with the prompt temperature = prompt.config.get("temperature", 0) # 4. Promote a tested version, or roll back by moving the label langfuse.update_prompt(name="support/triage", version=7, new_labels=["production"]) 1 Fetch by name and label The app never hard-codes prompt text, so improvements need no redeploy. 2 Compile Variables declared in the template are filled at run time. 3 Config travels with the prompt Model parameters are versioned alongside the text. 4 Promotion is a label move Rollback is the same call with the previous version number.

Slide 14: Governance and Security

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Governance and Security A shared library is shared risk; manage it deliberately Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 14 Access control Separate who can edit from who can publish; protect the production label. Review and approval Production changes need a second reviewer, as with code. No secrets in prompts Keys, credentials and internal URLs stay in configuration, never in templates. Assume prompts can leak OWASP added System Prompt Leakage in 2025: enforce rules in code, not only in the prompt. Defend against injection Prompt injection is OWASP's #1 LLM risk: delimit untrusted input, validate outputs, limit tool permissions. Audit trail Record who changed what and when; link every output to its prompt version.

Slide 17: Best Practices

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Best Practices For prompt engineering and for running a library Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 17 1 Define objectives clearly Know the desired outcome and write success criteria before drafting. 2 Iterate and test Improve against a fixed test set and real feedback, one change at a time. 3 Leverage variables Placeholders for dynamic content; fixed instructions stay fixed. 4 Document results Record eval scores, changelogs and known limits for every version. 5 Collaborate Share designs, review each other's prompts, and reuse common blocks. 6 Version and pin Promote with labels; pin exact versions where risk is high.

Slide 18: Starting Your Prompt Library

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Starting Your Prompt Library A practical path in five steps Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 18 1 Inventory Find prompts in code, notebooks and docs; rank by usage and risk. 2 Standardize Adopt one entry format: owner, variables, model settings, changelog. 3 Add evaluations Build golden test sets for the most-used prompts first. 4 Centralize Move entries into a registry or Git repo; apps fetch by label. 5 Govern and grow Review rules, usage metrics, and retirement of unused entries. Start small: a handful of high-traffic prompts with owners and test sets beats a large, unmaintained catalogue.

Slide 19: Key Takeaways

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Key Takeaways Craft the prompt, reuse the template, manage the library Prompt Engineering, Templates and Prompt Libraries 19 1 Prompts need clarity, context, structure, specificity and iteration. 2 Templates turn good prompts into reusable patterns with variables. 3 Libraries add ownership, versioning, evaluation and governance on top. 4 Deploy with labels, evaluate every version, and roll back in seconds. 5 Treat prompts as shared assets: secure them, document them, and retire what isn't used.

Frequently asked questions

What is a prompt library?

A prompt library is a searchable collection of prompts and templates organized by task or domain. It adds shared ownership, version history, evaluation evidence, and governance to reusable prompt designs.

How do prompts, templates, and libraries differ?

A prompt guides one task. A template provides a reusable structure with variable inputs. A library manages those structures across teams and applications.

What should a library entry contain?

Include an identifier, owner, description, tags, declared variables, template text, tested model settings, evaluation results, and a changelog. Environment labels can point to approved versions.

How do versions and labels work?

Versions preserve snapshots of the prompt and its configuration. Labels such as staging and production point to selected versions. Moving a label changes the selected version; exact version pins support reproducible use.

How should teams evaluate library prompts?

Evaluate quality, output format, safety, cost, and latency on representative test inputs. Record results for each version and model change, compare with the production baseline, and review changes before promotion.

How do I start a prompt library?

Inventory frequently used prompts, assign owners, standardize the entry format, add test sets, centralize approved versions, and establish review and retirement practices. Start with a small collection that the team can maintain.
